5511:
The typical Iron Age Israelite dwelling was the 'four-room' or pillared house: a central open or roofed space flanked by rows of pillars, side rooms for animals and storage, and a broad room at the back. Livestock were stabled on the ground floor and the family lived and slept largely upstairs or on the roof. Roofs were flat, made of beams covered with branches and packed clay, and were used for drying produce, sleeping and prayer, so the law required a parapet (Deut 22:8). Rahab hid the spies among flax on her roof (Josh 2:6), Samuel spoke with Saul on a roof (1 Sam 9:25-26), and Peter prayed on one in Joppa (Acts 10:9).

In first-century Galilean villages such as Capernaum, houses were built of local basalt with roofs of beams and clay, grouped in blocks of rooms around shared courtyards where related families cooked and worked. Friends of a paralytic could dig through such a roof to lower him down (Mark 2:4); Luke, writing for readers used to tiled roofs, mentions tiles (Luke 5:19). One room at Capernaum was venerated by Christians as Peter's house from an early date and later enclosed by an octagonal church. Many homes had a guest room or upper room (*katalyma*), the word used for the room of the Last Supper (Luke 22:11-12) and, many scholars argue, in Luke 2:7, suggesting Jesus was laid in the animals' area of a crowded family house rather than turned away from a commercial inn.

In cities, the poor lived in multi-storey apartment blocks (*insulae*) with shops on the ground floor; Eutychus fell from a third-storey window (Acts 20:9). The wealthy lived in a *domus* arranged around an atrium and dining room. The earliest churches met in houses, such as those of Priscilla and Aquila, Nympha and Philemon (Rom 16:5; Col 4:15; Phlm 1:2), which limited a congregation to perhaps a few dozen people. The oldest securely identified house church, at Dura-Europos in Syria, dates from the 230s-250s.

Clothing was basic. Men and women wore a tunic (Hebrew *kuttonet*, Greek *chiton*) of wool or linen and an outer cloak (*simlah*, *himation*) that doubled as a blanket; if taken in pledge it had to be returned by night (Exod 22:26-27; Deut 24:12-13). Jesus' teaching on giving the cloak as well as the tunic assumes these two garments (Matt 5:40), and soldiers gambled for his seamless tunic (John 19:23-24). Israelite men wore tassels on the corners of their cloaks (Num 15:37-41; Matt 9:20), the pious wore phylacteries (Matt 23:5), and wool and linen were not to be mixed (Deut 22:11). Purple dye from murex shellfish was a luxury, the trade of Lydia (Acts 16:14) and the mark of the rich man (Luke 16:19). People 'girded their loins' by tucking the tunic into a belt for work or running (1 Kgs 18:46; Luke 12:35), and tore their clothes or wore sackcloth in grief (Gen 37:34).

5525: Before coinage, silver was weighed in shekels; by the New Testament era Roman, Greek and Jewish coins circulated side by side. Converting biblical sums and measures into everyday terms reveals the force of many texts.
5526:
For most of the Old Testament period there were no coins. Silver and gold were weighed on balances using stone weights, and 'shekel' was a unit of weight, about 11.4 g in Judah on the evidence of inscribed weights. Abraham weighed out 400 shekels of silver for the cave of Machpelah (Gen 23:16), and Jeremiah weighed 17 shekels for a field at Anathoth (Jer 32:9-10). Fifty shekels made a mina (Ezekiel gives sixty) and a talent was 3,000 shekels, about 34 kg (Exod 38:25-26; Ezek 45:12). Dishonest merchants kept two sets of weights, which the prophets condemned (Amos 8:5; Prov 11:1). Coinage, invented in Lydia in the seventh century BC, reached Judah under Persia: the gold daric appears in Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 2:69; Neh 7:70-72), and small silver 'Yehud' coins were minted in the fourth century.

In Jesus' day the denarius, a Roman silver coin of about 3.9 g, was a day's wage for a laborer (Matt 20:2). The Greek drachma was roughly equal (Luke 15:8). The temple tax of two drachmas was the didrachma (Matt 17:24), and a stater or tetradrachm, in practice the Tyrian shekel, paid it for two people (Matt 17:27). The thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas were probably Tyrian shekels, echoing the price of a slave and Zechariah's prophecy (Matt 26:15; Exod 21:32; Zech 11:12-13). Small bronze coins included the assarion, a sixteenth of a denarius, for which two sparrows were sold (Matt 10:29), and the lepton, the smallest Jewish coin; the widow's two lepta made a quadrans, a sixty-fourth of a denarius (Mark 12:42).

Larger sums: a mina was 100 drachmas, about four months' wages (Luke 19:13); a talent was 6,000 denarii, some twenty years' wages for a laborer. The servant forgiven 10,000 talents, an unpayable sum of about sixty million denarii, refuses to forgive a debt of 100 denarii (Matt 18:24-28). Mary's nard was worth over 300 denarii, a year's wages (Mark 14:5; John 12:5), Philip reckoned 200 denarii would not feed the five thousand (John 6:7), and the good Samaritan left two denarii, about two days' wages, for the innkeeper (Luke 10:35).

Length was measured by the body: the cubit, elbow to fingertip, about 44.5 cm (a longer royal cubit was about 52 cm), the span (half a cubit), the handbreadth and the finger. Noah's ark measured 300 by 50 by 30 cubits (Gen 6:15) and Goliath six cubits and a span, about 2.9 m (1 Sam 17:4). The Greek stadion was about 185 m (Luke 24:13), the Roman mile about 1,480 m (Matt 5:41), and the fathom about 1.85 m (Acts 27:28). Dry measures included the ephah, perhaps 22 liters though estimates vary, the omer, a tenth of an ephah (Exod 16:36), and the homer of ten ephahs (Ezek 45:11). The bath, a liquid measure equal to the ephah, and the hin and log measured oil and wine. The stone jars at Cana held two or three measures each, perhaps 80-120 liters (John 2:6).

5552: Most people in Israel lived by farming grain, vines and olives under a climate of winter rains and dry summers. The agricultural year shaped the festivals, the prophets' imagery and Jesus' parables.
5553:
Israel has two seasons: a rainy winter and a dry summer. The 'early rain' (*yoreh*) in October and November softened the ground for ploughing and sowing; winter rains followed; the 'latter rain' (*malqosh*) in March and April filled out the grain before harvest (Deut 11:14; Joel 2:23; Jas 5:7). From May to September there was virtually no rain, and summer crops depended on heavy dew (Hos 14:5). Unlike Egypt with its Nile, the land 'drinks water by the rain from heaven', which made Israel's farmers dependent on God's provision and vulnerable to drought as covenant curse (Deut 11:10-17; 1 Kgs 17:1).

The Gezer calendar, a schoolboy's limestone tablet from about the tenth century BC, lists the farming year: two months of ingathering (olives), two of sowing grain, two of late sowing, a month of hoeing flax, a month of barley harvest, a month of harvest and measuring (wheat), two months of vine tending, and a month of summer fruit. Barley ripened around Passover in April (Ruth 1:22) and wheat around Pentecost in May-June; grapes were picked in late summer and olives in autumn, around the Feast of Booths. Figs ripened in early summer and late summer; Mark notes that when Jesus cursed the fig tree 'it was not the season for figs' (Mark 11:13).

Grain was cut with sickles, carried to a threshing floor where oxen or sledges trampled it (Deut 25:4; 1 Cor 9:9), and winnowed by tossing it into the evening breeze with a fork so the chaff blew away (Ruth 3:2; Ps 1:4; Matt 3:12). Gideon threshed wheat in a winepress to hide it from raiders (Judg 6:11). David bought Araunah's threshing floor, later the temple site (2 Sam 24:18-25). Elisha was ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah called him (1 Kgs 19:19). Reapers left corners and gleanings for the poor (Lev 19:9-10). Normal yields were perhaps five to ten times the seed, so harvests of thirty, sixty and a hundredfold were extraordinary (Gen 26:12; Mark 4:8).

Vineyards required terraces, a hedge, a watchtower and a winepress, and Isaiah's song of the vineyard uses each detail (Isa 5:1-7), as does Jesus' parable of the tenants, which reflects absentee landowners and tenant farmers common in first-century Galilee (Mark 12:1-12). Olives were crushed in presses; the name Gethsemane probably means 'oil press' (Mark 14:32). Amos was a herdsman and dresser of sycamore figs (Amos 7:14). The land was to rest every seventh year (Lev 25:3-4). Jesus drew constantly on this world: sowing on different soils, mustard seed, weeds among wheat, fields white for harvest (Mark 4:3-32; Matt 13:24-30; John 4:35).

5569: Ancient people faced high infant mortality, chronic infections, parasites and eye disease, with limited medical help. Healing stories in scripture, and the place of physicians, make most sense against this background.
5570:
Life expectancy at birth in the Roman world was perhaps twenty to thirty years, mainly because so many infants and children died; those who reached adulthood often lived into their fifties or sixties, and the psalmist's seventy or eighty years was a full life (Ps 90:10). Common afflictions included malaria, tuberculosis, dysentery and other gut infections, intestinal parasites, which have been identified in ancient Jerusalem latrines, and eye diseases such as trachoma that left many blind. Disability usually meant poverty and begging (Mark 10:46; John 9:8; Acts 3:2).

The 'leprosy' of the Bible (Hebrew *tsara'at*, Greek *lepra*) covered a range of skin conditions, and even mold in garments and houses, defined by visible symptoms and ritual impurity (Lev 13-14). It was not limited to Hansen's disease, though DNA from a first-century burial shroud in a tomb near Jerusalem has shown that true leprosy was present. Sufferers lived outside the camp or town (Lev 13:45-46; Luke 17:12), which made Jesus' touching a leper striking (Mark 1:40-42). Naaman's healing in the Jordan shows how foreign the condition's cure was to normal means (2 Kgs 5:1-14).

Remedies included olive oil and wine on wounds (Luke 10:34; Isa 1:6), balm from Gilead (Jer 8:22), a poultice of figs on Hezekiah's boil (2 Kgs 20:7), and a little wine for the stomach (1 Tim 5:23). Saliva was thought to have healing power, and Jesus sometimes used it (Mark 8:23; John 9:6). Greek medicine in the Hippocratic tradition was practised by trained physicians, often slaves or freedmen, and Luke is called 'the beloved physician' (Col 4:14). Physicians could be costly and unsuccessful, as the woman who spent all she had and only grew worse shows (Mark 5:26). The Chronicler criticizes Asa for seeking physicians rather than the LORD (2 Chr 16:12), while Ben Sira honors physicians as God's provision.

The sick also sought gods. Shrines of Asclepius, the Greek god of healing, flourished at Pergamum, Corinth and elsewhere, with patients sleeping in the sanctuary hoping for a cure, and some scholars connect the pool of Bethesda with such healing practices (John 5:2-9). Many assumed that illness was punishment for sin, a view Job's story and Jesus both resist (John 9:1-3), though scripture also links some sickness with sin (John 5:14; 1 Cor 11:30). The gospels distinguish illness from demon possession while recording both (Mark 1:32-34). James instructs the sick to call the elders for prayer and anointing with oil (Jas 5:14-16). Whether miraculous healing continues today is part of the cessationism debate.

5583: Only a minority in the ancient world could read and write fluently, but teaching through the family, the synagogue and memorization meant that many knew scripture well. Greek education produced the rhetorical skills visible in the New Testament letters.
5584:
Scholars distinguish several levels of literacy: recognizing letters, signing one's name, reading simple texts, and composing or copying at length. William Harris' influential study (*Ancient Literacy*, 1989) estimated that only about 10-15 percent of people in the Roman empire could read and write at a functional level, and Catherine Hezser suggested still lower figures for Jews in Roman Palestine. Others argue that Jewish emphasis on Torah reading raised literacy among men, at least for reading scripture aloud. The question is debated, but in any case most people learned by hearing.

In ancient Israel teaching began at home: parents were to impress the commands on their children, talk of them at home and on the road, and write them on doorposts (Deut 6:6-9; Prov 1:8). Abecedaries, alphabet practice texts, have been found at Izbet Sartah and Tel Zayit, and the tenth-century Gezer calendar may be a writing exercise. In one of the Lachish letters from about 588 BC an officer indignantly insists he can read a letter himself. Professional scribes handled royal and legal documents (Jer 32:10-12). Later rabbinic tradition credits Simeon ben Shetah and the high priest Joshua ben Gamla with founding schools for children, though the reliability of these reports is debated.

In the first century, synagogues were centers of instruction, and memorization was central: students learned large blocks of text by heart and teachers taught in memorable forms such as parallelism and parables. Jesus could read the Isaiah scroll in the synagogue (Luke 4:16-20), yet people asked how he had learning without having studied, meaning formal training under a rabbi (John 7:15). The council saw Peter and John as 'uneducated, common men', meaning without scribal training (Acts 4:13). Paul was educated 'at the feet of Gamaliel' in Jerusalem (Acts 22:3), and Timothy knew the scriptures from childhood through his mother and grandmother (2 Tim 1:5; 2 Tim 3:15).

Greek education moved from the elementary teacher (reading, writing, arithmetic) to the *grammaticus* (literature, especially Homer) to the rhetor (persuasive speech). A slave *paidagogos* escorted and supervised boys, an image Paul uses for the law (Gal 3:24-25). Paul's letters use rhetorical forms, though critics said his speech was unimpressive (2 Cor 10:10). Since most could not read, letters were read aloud to congregations (Col 4:16; 1 Thess 5:27), and Revelation blesses 'the one who reads aloud' and those who hear (Rev 1:3). Paul asks for his books and parchments (2 Tim 4:13).

5595: Jews buried their dead quickly, in family tombs, with mourning rituals that lasted days or weeks; in the late Second Temple period bones were later gathered into ossuaries. These customs shape the narratives of Lazarus and of Jesus' burial and resurrection.
5596:
Burial normally took place the same day as death, both because of the climate and because corpses caused impurity (Num 19:11-16; Acts 5:6-10). Israelites were buried in family tombs, and to be 'gathered to one's people' or 'to sleep with one's fathers' reflected this (Gen 25:8; 1 Kgs 2:10). Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah gave his family a burial place in the land, where Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob were laid (Gen 23:17-20; Gen 49:29-32). Iron Age Judean tombs were rock-cut chambers with benches on which bodies were laid; later, bones were moved to a repository to make room. Two tiny silver amulets from a tomb at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, from around 600 BC, carry the priestly blessing and are the oldest known texts of a biblical passage (Num 6:24-26).

In the late Second Temple period wealthier Jerusalem families used rock-cut tombs with long niches (*kokhim*) or arched benches. The body was washed, anointed with spices and wrapped in linen (John 19:39-40; Acts 9:37); Nicodemus brought about a hundred Roman pounds, roughly 33 kg, of myrrh and aloes, a royal quantity. About a year later the bones were gathered into a stone box called an ossuary, a practice common from about 20 BC to AD 70; ossuaries inscribed with names such as Caiaphas have been found. Tombs were sealed with stones; large round rolling stones like the one in the gospels were relatively rare and mostly used for wealthy tombs (Mark 15:46; Mark 16:3-4). Tombs were whitewashed before Passover so pilgrims would avoid impurity, the image behind Jesus' 'whitewashed tombs' (Matt 23:27).

Mourning was loud and public. Mourners tore their clothes, wore sackcloth, put dust or ashes on their heads and fasted (Gen 37:34; 2 Sam 1:11-12). Families hired professional mourning women and flute players (Jer 9:17-18; Matt 9:23). An intense mourning period lasted seven days (Gen 50:10), with a longer thirty days for great figures like Moses (Deut 34:8). Friends came to comfort the bereaved, as at Bethany (John 11:19). Lazarus had been in the tomb four days, past any doubt that he was dead (John 11:17; John 11:39).

Romans practised both cremation, dominant in the first century, and inhumation, which became standard by the late second century; poorer people joined burial clubs that paid for funerals and niches in shared tombs. Christians, following Jewish practice and their hope of resurrection, buried their dead, and from the late second century began using underground catacombs around Rome. The New Testament describes death as sleep for believers and grounds hope in Christ's bodily resurrection (1 Thess 4:13-18; 1 Cor 15:20-23; 1 Cor 15:42-44). The site of Jesus' tomb is traditionally the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which has strong early tradition; the Garden Tomb, proposed in the nineteenth century, is an Iron Age tomb and less likely historically.
